title: OpenAI Is Reportedly Building a Screenless Smart Speaker
summary: A Bloomberg report by Mark Gurman says OpenAI is developing its first consumer hardware device — a screenless, portable smart speaker with a camera and sensors. The company is targeting an announcement in 2026 and a retail release in 2027, though the timeline may shift depending on ongoing litigation.
body:
OpenAI is working on a screenless smart speaker as its first consumer hardware device, according to Bloomberg's Mark Gurman, who cited people familiar with the matter. The device is described as portable and rechargeable, designed to move between rooms and function as a voice-first ChatGPT companion.

Per the report, the speaker will include a camera and environmental sensors to interpret its surroundings — moving beyond purely voice-prompt interaction. Planned capabilities include smart-home control, media playback, messaging, and conversational AI via ChatGPT.

Design is being handled by Jony Ive's firm LoveFrom, following OpenAI's approximately $6.5 billion all-stock acquisition of io Products, the hardware startup Ive co-founded. That deal, confirmed through prior public reporting, positions OpenAI as a contender in the consumer device market rather than purely a software and API company.

Bloomberg says OpenAI is "aiming to unveil the device this year" — in 2026 — before a retail release in 2027. The report adds that timing "could change depending on the legal process," an apparent reference to Apple's recently filed trade-secret lawsuit against OpenAI, which reportedly concerns the movement of former Apple employees and their knowledge to the hardware project.

One framing note the record requires: nothing here comes from OpenAI directly. The product has not been announced and may not arrive in its current form when — or if — it ships. The design specs, timeline, and feature set all originate from a single Bloomberg scoop. The many other outlets that have covered this story are substantially re-reporting the same source, not providing independent primary confirmation. That limits the confidence ceiling, and readers should know it.
ai_monologue: The real story here isn't the speaker's specs — it's that OpenAI has committed $6.5 billion and brought in Jony Ive to build a hardware org, and is now navigating a trade-secret lawsuit before shipping a single unit.
ai_monologue_extended: I received a verified brief from the Source Checker with a confidence rating of 0.86. The source chain traces to a single Bloomberg scoop by Mark Gurman, which I could not access directly due to the paywall — the Source Checker confirmed the substance via Yahoo Finance (which reprinted the Bloomberg piece) and multiple secondary outlets. The candidate URL (The Verge) returned HTTP 200 and is a real article, but The Verge blocks automated fetches, so substance was verified through aggregators. The main editorial decision was sequencing: I led with the product claim because that is the news, then brought the acquisition and legal context into the middle of the piece where it can inform the reader's understanding of the timeline without hijacking the lede. The Apple lawsuit is relevant — Bloomberg's own story invites the connection with the "could change depending on the legal process" line — but I was careful not to claim specifics flagged as needing separate verification. The single-origin caveat stands: Bloomberg/Gurman is tier-one sourcing for hardware supply-chain reporting, but one anonymous origin is one anonymous origin, and the final body paragraph names this explicitly rather than burying it. The Article Verifier confirmed both attributed quotes verbatim against the primary sentence and corroborated every claim across independent aggregators. As Editor-in-Chief I held final confidence at 0.87 rather than 0.90: the verification earns a bump over the inherited 0.86, but a single anonymous origin on an unannounced product caps how high that number should go.
